en: *Gaṇakārikā*, 1:
"The fivefold groups are to be known as eight, and the group consists of three.
[The term *pañcaka* refers to collections delimited by the number five, such as gain (*lābha*) and so forth; by excluding any fewer or more than these, the author states the number as "eight."]

The word *tu* (but/however) emphasizes that the thorough knowledge of both the concise and the detailed [expositions] yields an equal result; thus, the commencement of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is meaningful in accordance with the disciple’s desire for inquiry. They are to be "known specifically" (*vijñeyāḥ*), meaning they must be understood in detail and reinforced through repeated practice, so that when the mind is always established in the meaning of the treatise, no fault regarding the discourse on Brahman (*brahmodya*) occurs even if the literal text is forgotten.
For otherwise, for one unable to perform [the practice], the sin would be equal to that of drinking liquor.
(GkT 1.1ab:4) The word *gaṇa* signifies a collection.
(GkT 1.1ab:5) By means of the conjunction *ca*, it should be understood that there are eight groups of five (*pañcaka*) alone, and one group (*gaṇa*) consisting of three (*trika*). (GkT 1.1ab:6)
The word "one" (*eka*) is used for the purpose of dispelling the doubt regarding the number eight mentioned immediately prior.
A "triad" (*trika*) is a collection delimited by the number three.

That very [triad] is the "self" (*ātman*), meaning the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), of the group of livelihoods such as begging; thus it is so described for the purpose of excluding other modes of livelihood.
Thus, these nine groups have been indicated as objects to be known.
He who correctly comprehends them will certainly reach the end of suffering and will become capable of bestowing favor upon others. Why, then, is this determined?

For it is determined by all the supreme yogis that the knower of this group of nine is called the Guru, the one who performs the consecration (*saṃskartā*). [The root] *vid* means "to know. Although the form would have been *veditā*, the Vedic usage *vettā* was employed to avoid breaking the meter.

Alternatively, in the context of investigation (*vicāraṇa*), the term "knower" (*vettā*) is used [to mean the one who investigates]. "Knower" means the investigator. Although the plural form "of the nine groups" (*navagaṇānām*) would have been expected, it was stated as "of the nine-group" (*navagaṇasya*) either to avoid breaking the meter or to indicate that the thorough knowledge of them yields distinct results.
The word "gaṇa" is also seen in the case of Nandin, Mahākāla, and others; therefore, the term "of this" (*asya*) was stated in order to dispel that doubt.
This means "of this [initiate] just mentioned," such as one who has attained [the goal] and so forth.
One who purifies a well-examined Brāhmaṇa—purifying the disciple by means of a specific initiation and a specific knowledge of the fivefold object—is called a "purifier" (*saṃskartṛ*).
And he is called, above all, a "Guru" by those who know [the truth].

(GkT 1.1ab) The meaning is that the Guru, the Teacher, destroys the sins and produces a preeminent merit even for those endowed with faith who merely see or converse with him, provided they belong to the various stages of life (*āśrama*).
Alternatively, the connection between the verses is demonstrated in another way. (GkT 1.1ab)

Indeed, it is heard here that there are two kinds of Brahmins who attain liberation (*apavarga*): the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and the teacher (*ācārya*). Among these, in this system, the practitioner who desires to go to liberation, having heard the scripture or having learned the nature of the injunctions and so forth from the mere instruction of a teacher, must perform the practice of the yoga of injunction with extreme diligence.
He states what must be done by one who, being a teacher (*ācārya*), desires to attain liberation (*apavarga*):

"The fivefold groups (*pañcaka*) are to be known as eight, and the group consisting of three is one. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates that the nine groups are to be understood through the determination of the introduction (*upodghāta*) and so forth of the entire sūtra and its constituent parts.
Having understood that, he indicates this specific point: "A refinement (saṃskāra) must be performed by one who dispels the ignorance arising from the doubts of his disciples.
The remaining meaning of the individual words is as before.
But how is this understood?
It is understood that one who desires for oneself the status of a teacher on account of [removing] suffering must specifically know the nine groups [of deities], because: [GkT_1.1ab:34]

The knower of this group of nine and the one who performs its consecration is called the Guru. Furthermore, even if one is unable to be intent upon such practice, if they become endowed with faith and, while observing at least a small portion of the rules, do not abandon the cultivation of knowledge, then they go to liberation and are called an Ācārya.

"But he who is satisfied merely by knowing the meaning of the scriptures, being devoid of faith and so forth—or even if possessed of a mere measure of faith and so forth—yet lacking the knowledge of [the true nature of] gain and so on, is indeed a mere semblance of a teacher (*ācāryābhāsa*) and does not go to liberation.
Therefore, the true nature of the *gaṇa* must be stated.
To the question, "Who are the eight pentads (*pañcaka*), and what is the group consisting of the triad (*trika*)?", he says: [He states: GkT_1.1cd:4]
Acquisitions, impurities, means, regions, states, purifications, the eight powers of the initiator, the five triads, and the three modes of conduct.

*Acquisition (lābha) is that which is being accomplished as the fruit of the means; or alternatively, acquisitions are distinguished by the divisions of knowledge, austerity, devotion to the deity, stability, and supernatural power; or alternatively, they are entities previously unmanifested that become manifest within the self of the practitioner.*
These are the gains.
Those states dependent upon the self for whose destruction the practitioner exerts effort are the impurities (*mala*).
Alternatively, the impurities are divided into five types: false knowledge, unrighteousness, attachment, the state of being bound (transmigration), and the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*).
The means (*upāya*) are those which are most effective for the practitioner and are the causes of purification and increase.
Alternatively, the means are distinguished by the divisions of dwelling, conduct, recitation, meditation, constant mindfulness, and serenity.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to complete the meter, or it indicates that [this sūtra] sets forth the characteristics of attainment and the others as being mutually distinct.

"Places (*deśa*), states (*avasthā*), and purifications (*viśuddhi*)" is a copulative compound (*dvandva*). (GkT 1.2:7) By the power of which [places] as their support, the practitioner attains purity and growth; those places—characterized as the assembly of gurus, mountain caves, cremation grounds, and the [liṅga of] Rudra—we shall describe. (GkT 1.2:8) The "states" (*avasthā*) are the stages established within the single limit from the attainment of non-attainment for the practitioner; they will be described as distinguished by specific features such as the Manifest (*vyakta*) and so forth. (GkT 1.2:9)
The purifications (*viśuddhi*) consist in the absolute removal of false knowledge and the rest;
and there is a copulative compound (*dvandva*) consisting of the powers that effect initiation (*dīkṣā*).

Those which have initiation as their cause are the "effectors of initiation" (*dīkṣākārīṇi*); they are designated as substance, time, action, form, and teacher, and residing within the person of the practitioner, they are the causes for the engagement in the means [to liberation].
The powers (*balāni*) are characterized by devotion to the Guru, great grace, victory over the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*), and non-negligence (*apramāda*).
(GkT 1.2:13) "Eight pentads"—this is the concluding summary.
(GkT 1.2:14) Regarding the phrase "three modes of conduct" (*tisro vṛttayaḥ*), the Vedic usage *trīṇi vṛttayaḥ* was employed for the sake of lightening the fifth syllable [of the meter]. (GkT 1.2:15)

The modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*) that do not contradict the scriptures are those known as begging for alms (*bhaikṣa*), eating what is discarded (*utsṛṣṭa*), and accepting whatever is obtained (*yathālabdha*).
Among these, first, for one in the initial stage, the mode of livelihood is exclusively begging for alms; the rule for this is stated as follows:

Having recognized the time for begging, having become pure, having washed both hands with ashes, and having taken up the vessel, one should wash it with water and purify it. Then, having prostrated before Mahādeva, one should request his permission.

Thereafter, regarding the phrase "the gurus": then, permitted by the gods and the gurus, either reciting the mantras or with his mind fixed on the Lord (Īśvara), he should proceed along a path purified by his gaze, avoiding the houses of those who have been cursed or fallen,
and any place where there are causes for fear, or foul omens such as crows and the like, or impurity due to the presence of naked women, excrement, wicked people, or beggars.

If [food] is obtained, he should avoid even those houses and wander through one or another of the villages and so forth; however, if he does not obtain enough in the interval, or if some obstacle arises, then having returned to his own abode, performed an expiation (prāyaścitta) according to the offense,
and consecrated it with mantras, he should offer that alms-food to Śiva and to his Guru.

Having fixed Maheśvara in his heart, with speech restrained, facing either north or east, and having established a state of equanimity (*samarasa*), he should eat, placing [the food] higher and higher. Regarding the vessel and the purification of the vessel, these should be understood as authorized by the Sūtras and established in the Smṛtis.
And likewise Yājñavalkya says:
"The vessels of an ascetic are made of clay, bamboo, wood, or gourd;
their purification is by means of water and scrubbing with cow-hair."
Manu also said:
"His vessels should be non-metallic and free from cracks;
their purification with water is prescribed, just as that of the *camasa* cups in a sacrifice. (GkT 1.2:22)
"Whatever [food] may be contaminated by a corpse, smeared with impurity, or even split open—
having eaten or drunk such things there, an ascetic (yati) shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Thus says Yama.

Because of the inclusion of the phrase "not contradicting the scriptures," the prohibition should be understood as applying to alms obtained for purposes such as proclaiming knowledge, teaching, or maintaining worldly conduct; this is the rule for one in the state of a *prātipada*.
This same rule also applies to one in the third stage.
* Herein, this much is the distinction:

*GkT_1.2:27* one in the third stage does not perform the rites such as the announcement of the penance (*prāyaścitta*), the recitation of the five Brahmans (*pañcabrahma-japa*), or the ritual bathing (*anusnāna*) and so forth, because of being a supreme yogi (*paramayogitva*). *GkT_1.2:28* For one in the second stage, the mode of life (*vṛtti*) is indeed that which has been relinquished. *GkT_1.2:29*

If someone of non-defiled birth should give food and drink intended for the gods and others, or given out of compassion or curiosity, provided it is free from defects such as impurity—that is "discarded" (utsṛṣṭa).
And that should be consumed by means of the differentiation of Māyā.
There is no restriction regarding the vessel once one has desisted from begging alms.

The livelihood of one in the fourth stage is "as obtained. (GkT 1.2:33) That food and drink which is acquired day by day, or over two or three days, while remaining in a cremation ground, is called "as obtained.
(GkT 1.2:34) However, for one in the fifth stage, because the body no longer exists, the possibility of a livelihood is precluded. (GkT 1.2:35)

Considering that the sequence of the text is not of primary importance and that the knowledge of the meaning alone is what is essential, he provides the exposition out of order, beginning with "Devotion to the Guru" (gurubhakti) and so forth.

Alternatively, since all undertakings are for the sake of gain, the gains were first mentioned at the outset in order to make known their primacy; now, however, [it is shown that] all gains are to be accomplished by means of methods (*upāya*), and those methods are to be practiced by persons who lack strength.
Since they cannot be overcome, he states at the outset the enumeration of the powers in order to make known their preeminence:
Devotion to the Guru, serenity of mind, victory over the pairs of opposites, as well as righteousness and vigilance—these are remembered as the fivefold power. (Gk 1.3)
The Guru is the teacher, the instructor of the knowledge of the fivefold reality (*pañcārtha*).
Devotion to him is faith; one who is overwhelmed by all sufferings should cultivate this conviction: "He alone is my savior.
Thus it has been said:

"The Guru is God, the Guru is Lord," and so forth; yet there is no contradiction between devotion and the [scriptural] teachings regarding the cause [of liberation], because devotion to those two is possible only through the Guru’s permission. (GkT 1.3:3) However, he who does not grant permission for such devotion to be performed is not a Guru at all, because he fails to act as a benefactor. (GkT 1.3:4) And that devotion to the Guru must be constantly cultivated by avoiding what is not intended by him and by performing services such as rising [to greet him] and the like. (GkT 1.3:5)
Having understood his intention, one should perform what is beneficial for him, even if it is not prescribed in the scriptures.
And so it has been said:
"To those who know the meaning of the texts," and so forth.

For whatever is intended by the Guru is indeed prescribed, and even if not explicitly stated in the scriptures, it becomes conducive to the highest good, just as was the case with Rāma’s slaying of his mother.

(GkT 1.3:8) Furthermore, the words of the Guru must be trusted, for otherwise faults are heard [in the scriptures], and there is the danger of failing to attain the knowledge of reality. (GkT 1.3:9) Indeed, one who lacks the strength of devotion may, despite being endowed with the capacity for grasping [the teachings] and so forth, understand the meaning of the scriptures erroneously due to the arrogance of [supposed] knowledge; therefore, for one endowed with the capacity for grasping and so forth, devotion alone is the true strength. (GkT 1.3:10)
Nor is there any contradiction with the Bhāṣya;
for the meaning of the statement "the eightfold power is celibacy" (*aṣṭāṅgaṃ brahmacaryam*) is as follows:

devotion alone is called the "eightfold" (*aṣṭāṅga*) because it is a limb (*aṅga*) of the eight [practices] beginning with seizing (*grahaṇa*), just as in the case of the term "limbs of the Veda" (*vedāṅga*), which denotes something distinct from the limbs themselves.

That very [state] is called "brahmacarya" because it is the cause of brahmacarya. If, on the other hand, its meaning were according to the literal sense [of the word], then there would be a contradiction with the indicative expressions such as "the provision of clothing" (*vāsovidhāna*) and so forth. He states the second power for one who is authorized in the ritual rule (*vidhi*).
"And clarity of the intellect" (prasādaś ca mateḥ). By the term "clarity of the intellect," freedom from turbidity is expressed.
For when that [freedom from turbidity] exists, the intellect becomes clear.
"And likewise, power is the state of being unclouded," so says the commentary (*bhāṣya*).
If that is so, why was it not explicitly stated here as well?

It was stated as "the state of being unclouded" with reference to the primary factor, for the purpose of making known that power also consists in the absence of impurity, delusion, and so forth, which are causes for the clarity of the intellect.

The word "ca" (and) indicates that although the previously mentioned power exists, its efficacy has already been realized; therefore, its status as a power is not considered here because of its primary [prior] nature.
Furthermore, that state of being unstained (*akaluṣatva*) is twofold: supreme and inferior.
Among these, even while the seed of stain exists, that which obstructs the arising of stain and extends as far as future stain is [the superior state].

That which does not arise for a certain period of time because it is free from turbidity is the lower [state]; that which, due to the exhaustion of the seeds, does not arise as turbidity even when the causes are present in their absolute entirety, is the higher [state].
This describes the third power of one authorized in the practice of yoga.

"Victory over the pairs, likewise" (GkT 1.3:26). The "pairs" (*dvandva*) are the means of suffering—namely, those pertaining to the internal (*ādhyātmika*), the external (*ādhibhautika*), and the celestial (*ādhidaivika*). "Victory" over them means endurance, that is to say, not being overwhelmed by the pairs. (GkT 1.3:27) The word "likewise" (*tathā*) has the sense of "similarly. (GkT 1.3:28)
Just as, even when the previously mentioned power exists, the power considered for one who is qualified by a rule that has not yet fulfilled its purpose is specifically his state of being untainted;
so too, even when two powers are present, the power considered primarily is specifically his capacity to endure the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*) which has not yet fulfilled its purpose.

That too is of two kinds, distinguished as superior and inferior. First, that which consists of the practice of meditation and so forth for a practitioner who is intent upon the performance of yoga while his sins have not yet been destroyed, and who must experience cold, heat, and other such conditions to a mild or moderate degree—that is the inferior [endurance]. Second, that which consists of the capacity to endure the pairs of opposites (*dvandvasahitva*), characterized by being unassailable even by extremely intense cold and so forth, for one who has gone to a cave or similar location once all sins have been entirely destroyed—that is the superior [endurance].

The author of the Bhāṣya, however, has explained that the nature of the cow and the deer refers only to the supreme [Self]. Intending that the students would understand the other qualities of the cow and the deer by inferring them from the quality of being free from impurity (*akaluṣatva*), he did not state them explicitly. Regarding the one who is devoted to constant mindfulness, he states the fourth power with the words, "And the Dharma itself."

The word *eva* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). The meaning is that when *dharma* alone is present, then there is strength. Even if there is the presence of a slight amount of *adharma*, there is no fault in the emphasis, just as one might say, "This cloth is white," even though a black speck is present.
The word "ca" (and) indicates that even when the three previously mentioned powers are present, the Dharma alone is the power because it has not yet been fully realized in practice.
Regarding the one who is established in the yoga of completion, he states the fifth power as "heedfulness" (*apramāda*).
What is intended here by "heedfulness" is specifically distinguished knowledge.
And thus the commentary on this [sūtra] states: "But he possesses knowledge, because it says 'he is vigilant'.

The word "and" (ca) indicates that when the body, senses, merit, and demerit have been excluded, vigilance alone is the power; it also excludes any notion of deficiency or superiority among the powers. "The power is fivefold" is the summary.
The word "remembered" (*smṛtam*) indicates that [the teaching] was spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*).

Now, one might object: consideration of power (*bala*) is appropriate in a case where, by accomplishing that [power], the destruction of an enemy becomes possible. However, here in this treatise on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*), for one who is free from passion and possesses no acquisitions (*niṣparigraha*), enemies do not exist at all; how then could there be their destruction? Therefore, consideration of power is inappropriate here.
This is not so.
Here too, because the destruction of the practitioner's enemies such as ignorance is logically established, he says the following in order to demonstrate that:
"With the destruction of ignorance, there is the destruction of unrighteousness and of that which causes attachment."
The loss of death, the abandonment of the state of being a bound soul (paśu), and purification are recorded as fivefold.

[Regarding the phrase "the abandonment of ignorance and unrighteousness" (*ajñānahānir adharmasya*): since this would have resulted in a metrical defect (*chandobhaṅga*), it was stated as "the abandonment of ignorance and [the abandonment] of unrighteousness" (*ajñānahāny-adharmasya*).
There is no fault here because it follows the archaic style of the seers (*ārṣatva*).]
And ignorance (*ajñāna*) is that which will be described hereafter; its destruction is the absolute eradication of it along with its seed (*sabīja*).
(GkT 1.4:3) Non-dharma (*adharma*) is also that which will be described hereafter; its destruction is the absolute eradication of it along with its modifications (*savikāra*).
(GkT 1.4:4) Just like non-dharma, the destruction of that which causes attachment (*saṅgakara*) is also explained. (GkT 1.4:5)
The word "ca" (and) serves to carry forward the term "loss" (*hāni*).
Indeed, the absolute eradication of "falling away" (*cyuti*), which will be described hereafter, together with its seed, is called the "loss of falling away.
Because the word "of the state of being a bound soul" (*paśutvasya*) is expressed in the genitive case, it is connected with the term "loss" mentioned immediately prior.

* Alternatively, according to the analogy of the hand-drum and the jewel (*ḍamarukamaṇinyāya*), the word "loss" (*hāni*) mentioned in the middle is connected with both "falling away" (*cyuti*) and "state of being a beast" (*paśutva*).
* Or, the particle "and" (*ca*), which was stated at the end of the preceding phrase [beginning with] "the cause of attachment," is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) here.
* It does not merely draw back the word "loss"; it also excludes any deficiency or excess among the purifications (*śuddhi*).
The absolute cessation of the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), resulting from its connection with the sovereignty of Maheśvara, is called the "abandonment of the state of being a bound soul.

(GkT 1.4:12) "Purification is fivefold" is the concluding summary. (GkT 1.4:13) "They are remembered" is stated for the purpose of demonstrating that they were spoken by a reliable authority (*āpta*). (GkT 1.4:14)
But do these cessations of enemies and powers belong to one who is differentiated by various states, or to one who is in a single state?
Why is there this doubt? Because both are observed, like the discus of Viṣṇu.
It is said: for the most part, they belong to one differentiated by various states, since [the author] speaks of a differentiation of states.
The Manifest, the Unmanifest, the Severing of Victory, and the Culmination is the fifth here;
indeed, the state of the Pratipad is called the state of the Manifest.
Why is that?

"In the Pāśupata [system], this [state] is called *avyakta* (unmanifest) because it is not the cause for the manifestation of individuality (*vyakti*), since instruction states that one is a bearer of the mark (*liṅgadhārī*) by means of ash-baths, lying down, subsequent baths, and so forth.
(GkT 1.5ab:3) "But the second state is called the *avyaktāvasthā* (unmanifest state) because it is not the cause for the manifestation of genus (*jāti*) and so forth.
(GkT 1.5ab:4) "Why? (GkT 1.5ab:5)
[This is] because of the instruction on unmanifest signs (*avyaktaliṅga*) and because of the instruction on the concealment of one's knowledge and so forth.

Furthermore, the third stage is called the "stage of victory" (*jayāvasthā*) because it serves the purpose of conquering the senses. Although this [stage] also has the constant devotion to the deity (*devanityatva*) as its own aim, the Teacher, the author of the Commentary, has stated that its primary purpose is indeed the conquest of the senses by way of explaining the connection between the aphorisms.
The state whose meaning is the conclusion of the cutting is called the "state of cutting" (*chedāvasthā*). The absolute cessation of all the practitioner’s activities is the "completion" (*niṣṭhā*).
The state characterized by that is called the "state of completion" (*niṣṭhāvasthā*).

The term "state" (*avasthā*) was not mentioned here by the author with the intention that, through the expression of qualifiers such as "manifest" (*vyakta*), there would arise a specific understanding of those [states] possessing the capacity for deliberation (*ūha*) and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the exclusion of both deficiency and excess.

If it is argued that the exclusion of excess is untenable because other states—such as those of a ghost (*preta*), a madman (*unmatta*), or a deluded person (*mūḍha*)—exist, we say no; for by the rule of concealment (*gopana*), they are included within the state of being unmanifest (*avyakta*) itself.

If it is argued that the states of *jayat* and *cheda* would also necessarily follow as being the unmanifest state (*avyaktāvasthā*), we say no; for these two do not admit the rule of concealment (*gopananiyama*). Without admitting the state of completion (*niṣṭhāvasthā*), they declare the state of perfection (*siddhāvasthā*) to be the fifth.
Some [opponents] refute that view by means of a restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) alone.
"And the fifth state here is indeed the final one" (GkT 1.5ab).

Here, within this system of five objects (*pañcārthadarśana*), it is understood from the authority of the aphorism that the fifth state is specifically the state of completion (*niṣṭhāvasthā*), and not the state of perfection (*siddhāvasthā*). In that regard, because there is no longer anything to be eliminated or attained, it is the states of the practitioner (*sādhakāvasthā*) that are described here, and nothing other than those.
Here he says:
It is illogical for one who lacks qualification to attain a [spiritual] state.

In that regard, just as the attainment of the second and subsequent states involves factors such as the non-turbidity of knowledge which bring about qualification, so too, what is the cause for the attainment of the first state? This is now explained.
In this context as well, initiation produced by specific causes is the cause.
Since it is for the purpose of explaining those causes that he says this:
"Substance, time, action, form, and the guru is indeed the fifth here. (GkT 1.5)
In this context, the various effects designated as *vidyā*, *kalā*, and *paśu* are called "substance" (*dravya*).
Among these, *vidyā* residing in the disciple is a constituent part of initiation (*dīkṣā*), by which the disciple becomes authorized for initiation;
whereas that *vidyā* residing in the teacher, by which the teacher brings the complete initiation to fruition, is the [other] *vidyā*.

The ritual components (*kalā*) such as *darbha* grass and so forth are parts of the initiation (*dīkṣā*). For it has been stated: "Furthermore, *darbha* grass, sacred ash, sandalwood paste, and likewise the thread, flowers, and incense—this is remembered as the sequence."
"The animal is to be consecrated as a Brāhmaṇa.
By explaining it in this way, the inclusion of the ritual implements and so forth is also secured; therefore, there is no contradiction with the *Saṃskārakārikā*.
The time is the forenoon.
The ritual action performed for the sake of purifying both the image (*mūrti*) and the disciple is called *saṃskārakarma*.
Its sequence should be observed in the *Saṃskārakārikā*.

By the word "image" (*mūrti*), that which was explained in the *Upahārasūtra* as the place of worship for Mahādeva—characterized by the vertical liṅga and so forth—is intended here as the area of ground to the right of it, unobstructed by walls or other such barriers.

The Guru is the Teacher; he is of two kinds, distinguished as the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). Among these, the lower is one who possesses the knowledge of the five subjects (*pañcārtha*) and adheres to the established limits [of the system].
And so it has been said:
He who is intent upon conduct that conforms to the scriptures, being of superior intellect and skillful,
is indeed considered by the wise to be a teacher (*ācārya*) and the cause of knowledge. Likewise:

Because he establishes his disciples in right conduct (*ācāra*), practices it himself, and gathers (*ācinoti*) the meanings of the scriptures, he is therefore celebrated as an *ācārya* (teacher). His presiding authority is the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, the supreme guru; and when this is thus described, the underlying cause (*nimitta*) is likewise not left unmentioned here.
The word "ca" (and) indicates the exclusion of what is deficient or excessive.
The word "eva" (only/itself) emphasizes the preeminence of the Guru.
The word "iha" (here) is a reference to one's own established doctrine (*siddhānta*).
"Five" is the conclusion.
Alternatively, by reversing the order of these two words here, another meaning is demonstrated:
"In this very Pāśupata system alone are there such specific causes for initiation, and not elsewhere."
And thus it is stated that the initiation (*dīkṣā*) to be accomplished here is indeed distinguished, and not elsewhere.
Now, is this initiation distinguished solely by its specific causes, or rather also by its specific fruits? For this reason, he says the following: [GkT 1.5cd–26]
Knowledge, austerity, constancy, steadfastness, and accomplishment as the fifth;

therein, the knowledge of reality concerning the five categories, by way of summary, expansion, division, distinction, synthesis, and conclusion, is the first acquisition of learning, which is called "knowledge.

Although the nature of these—summary and so forth—has been revealed by the venerable Teacher at the conclusion of his commentary, we shall nevertheless state it briefly for the purpose of explaining that commentary.
In this context, the enumeration (*uddeśa*) of categories is their concise statement (*samāsa*).

This [enumeration] is expressed by means of words and so forth, beginning with "the end of suffering" (*duḥkhānta*) and the rest. The detailed exposition (*vistara*) is the full description, according to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), of those categories already enumerated.
The phrase beginning with "patiḥ saṃnādya" [refers to the Lord].
By virtue of being the means to that [attainment], the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇas*) are also expressed by the word "vistara" (expansion).
"Vibhāga" (division) is the designation of the difference between properties (*dharma*) and the substrata (*dharmin*) according to their respective characteristics as they occur.
It is called "Abhidhāna" (the designation) because it is designated everywhere;
this should be understood through the etymological derivation from the root *dhā* with the prefix *abhi*.
In that regard, the classification of the End of Suffering (*duḥkhānta*) is first stated.

The removal of all suffering is the end of suffering (*duḥkhānta*). It is of two kinds: that which is without self (*anātmaka*) and that which possesses a self (*sātmaka*). Among these, the one without self is the absolute cessation of all sufferings; the one possessing a self, however, is the attainment (*siddhi*) characterized by the sovereignty of Maheśvara.
That power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is twofold: namely, the power of knowledge and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*).
Among these, the power of knowledge is simply knowledge itself as a power.

Although it is indeed one, it is said to be fivefold—by means of seeing, hearing, and so forth—due to the distinction between its objects taken collectively and individually; this is for the purpose of negating an imputed omniscience, such as that attributed to Brahmā and others.

The cause of action is power (*śakti*); it is the power of action, and it is threefold, distinguished by [the powers of] "swiftness like thought" (*manojavitva*) and so forth. Among these, "swiftness like thought" (*manojavitva*) is the state of acting with unsurpassed speed; "assumption of any form at will" (*kāmarūpitva*) is the presiding over the agency of subsequent forms by mere will, independent of karma and other factors; and "the nature of being free from the organs" (*vikaraṇadharmitva*) is the connection with unsurpassed sovereignty even while possessing a body and sense organs.
And thus:
when this twofold accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained, then there are ten characteristics of accomplishment, beginning with "independence" (*avaśyatva*) and ending with "falling" (*patitva*).
Among these, "independence" (*avaśyatva*) is the state of being unsurpassed and not subject to another's will.

"Now, what is this so-called state of non-submission (*avaśyatva*)? Some say: "When the stain of submissiveness (*vaśyatva-mala*) has ceased, a quality called non-submission, which resides in the Person (*puruṣa*), becomes manifest, just as whiteness is manifested in a cloth. But that is incorrect, because the manifestation of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) has been refuted, and because it is impossible for a quality that is not of the nature of the Self (*anātman*) to be manifested.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the nature of being non-self (anātmatva), and because it contradicts the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "when [the soul] is joined with the guṇas," there is no manifestation of something already existing;
rather, it is the very connection with sovereignty that is called "independence" (avaśyatva), since it effects the cessation of dependence on others.
Alternatively, when [the soul] is joined with the guṇas, it then becomes such as it was not before, like a snake or a loop of rope.

The state of that [subject] is its own nature; "inseparability" (*avaśyatva*) is stated here as a distinction for the sake of conventional usage. In this same manner, the analysis regarding "non-pervasibility" (*anāveśyatva*) and so forth should also be understood. Furthermore, since this has been elaborated upon by me in the investigation of the pre-existent effect (*satkārya*), it is not expanded upon here.

Inviolability is the state of being connected with a knowledge that cannot be overcome by other beings; indestructibility is the state of being devoid of life dependent upon other beings; fearlessness is the state of having transcended all fears; imperishability is the state of being eternally connected with sovereignty;

agelessness is the state of being absolutely unconnected with the result of physical or sensory deficiency; and freedom from suffering is the state of not being touched by the pain arising from the separation from the vital breaths and so forth.

Immortality is the state of being unimpeded even by Maheśvara in all activities directed toward desired objects; non-obstruction is the quality of being superior to all bound souls (paśus); greatness arises from the excellence of sovereignty; and lordship (pati-tva) is the state of being the master of all effects, such as the bound souls and so forth.
Whatever is dependent is an effect; its division is stated to be knowledge (*vidyā*), limited power (*kalā*), and the bound soul (*paśu*).

Among these, knowledge is said to be a quality of the bound soul according to the perspective of its own scripture (*svaśāstra*), whereas according to the Vaiśeṣika perspective, it is like a substance (*dravya*).

It is twofold, due to the distinction between the natures of consciousness (*bodha*) and non-consciousness (*abodha*). Among these, that which has the nature of non-consciousness is characterized by [the categories] beginning with *dharma*; it is included within *vidyā* because the inclusion of that whose essence is *avidyā* implies the inclusion of everything starting from *kalā*. On the other hand, that which has the nature of consciousness is said to be fourfold or fivefold according to the distinctions of its objects.

In terms of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), however, the functioning of consciousness (*vṛtti*) is twofold: the specific functioning (*viveka-vṛtti*) and the general functioning (*sāmānya-vṛtti*). Among these, the specific functioning is generally manifested through instruction (*upadeśa*), and there is no other designation for it. Indeed, "knowledge" (*vidyā*) is the specific designation; the general functioning, however, is manifested by the mere means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is called "mind" (*citta*).
The distinction between these two has been shown by me in another commentary and is not demonstrated here.
Being insentient while not resting upon consciousness is *kalā*.
That too is twofold: called "the effect" (*kārya*) and called "the instrument" (*karaṇa*).
In that regard, the effects (*kārya*) are tenfold, characterized by earth, water, fire, air, ether, smell, taste, form, touch, and sound;
whereas the instruments (*karaṇa*) are thirteenfold, namely the five organs of action, the five organs of cognition, and the three internal organs.
An animal (*paśu*) is that which is connected with the state of being an animal (*paśutva*).
It is also of two kinds: with impurity (*sāñjana*) and without impurity (*nirañjana*). Among these, that which is with impurity is connected with a body and sense organs, and is of fourteen types.
For it has been said: "The divine [realm] is to be known as eightfold, and that of the animal womb as fivefold;
the human state is a single stage—this is the circle of saṃsāra.
Thus, the stainless one is threefold: the withdrawn, the one who has attained liberation (kaivalya), and the one joined with the yoga of consummation (niṣṭhā-yoga).

The cause that effects the creation, destruction, and grace of the entire universe—though it is one, its division is described through the differentiation of its qualities and attributes by such statements as "the state of being the Lord is other [than the individual soul]," and so forth. Lordship (*patitva*) is the power of unsurpassed knowledge and action; being eternally connected with that sovereignty is existence (*sattva*);

having sovereignty that is not adventitious is primordiality (*ādyatva*); being devoid of all birth is non-arisenness (*ajātatva*); and being the agent of the great creation and destruction is the state of arising from *bhava* (*bhavodbhavatva*).

Supreme excellence is the state of being denoted by names that signify the qualities and attributes of reality; or, "leftwardness" (*vāmatva*) is the state of being denoted by names that signify the production of those dharmas which cause the end of suffering.

"Play" (*krīḍā*) is the essential nature of being the cause for the arising of all effects solely by one's own will. "Divinity" (*devatva*) is the possession of that [play] as one's attribute. "Sovereignty" (*paratva*) is the state of being superior to the *siddhas*, *sādhakas*, and *paśus*. "Eldership" (*jyeṣṭhatva*) is the state of being the first even at the beginning of creation. "Rudraship" (*rudratva*) is the state of being the one who instills fear through sound even at the beginning of creation, independent of karma and other such factors.

The state of being a *kāmin* is the capacity to perform all actions according to one's own will; the state of being a *śaṃkara* is the quality of bringing about peace, happiness, and liberation; the state of being *kāla* is the agency of dissolution even within the intermediate creation; the state of being a *kalavikaraṇa* is the power to join the *kalās*—known as effects and causes—with their respective locations, bodies, and so forth; and the state of being a *balapramathana* is the agency of granting, withholding, or interrupting the functioning of the powers of *dharma*, *adharma*, and the rest at will.

It is the state of being the agent of delight, passion, and perfuming for all gods, humans, and animals; the state of subduing all beings; the possession of equal power in both the differentiated (*sakala*) and undifferentiated (*niṣkala*) states; the state of being the mind of the mind; the presiding over infinite bodies that cause happiness (*aghoratva*); the presiding over infinite bodies that cause suffering (*ghorataratva*); the pervasive presiding over all effects such as the *vidyās*; and the fulfillment, which is the power to manifest infinite bodies and so forth according to one's desire.
Pauruṣya (the state of being the Puruṣa):

both of these are called the "puruṣatva" (state of being the Puruṣa) of the Blessed One. Greatness, divinity, and the state of being superior, more exalted, and distinct from all cattle and so forth have been previously mentioned.
The state of having the syllable *oṃ* as its single object of meditation, which serves as the cause for the end of suffering, is the nature of *oṃ*.
The state of being a *ṛṣi* is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), while the state of being a *vipra* is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
To make known that these two pervade their substratum, possess infinite objects, and are unsurpassed, it is said that "the Lord is Great" (*mahān*) because He is their substratum.

The Blessed One is said to be "this" because he exists at all times and in all places with an unchanging intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since words function by way of the door of qualities and attributes (*guṇadharma*), the Blessed One is called "pure" (*viśuddha*) because he is distinct from them and not differentiated by them. [He is] the supreme cause, endowed with eternal and innate sovereignty.
Where words turn back, that is proclaimed as the purity of speech. The ascetic who attains one-pointed concentration there, even for a single moment,
shall burn away all karmas and attain union with Śiva.

The bestowing of all sovereignty is *maheśvaratva* (the state of being the Great Lord); mastery over all effects is *īśatva* (the state of being the Lord); mastery over all branches of knowledge is *īśānatva* (the state of being the Sovereign); and mastery over all beings is *īśvaratva* (the state of being the Supreme Lord). Indeed, the meaning of these terms, beginning with *īśa*, has been demonstrated here in this way by taking their respective contexts into account; otherwise, however, they would possess exactly the same meaning.

Since the mention of "Brahman" is intended as an illustration, sovereignty over all lords is "adhipatitva" (lordship); expansion and vastness is "brahmatva" (the state of being Brahman); and complete fulfillment and contentment is "śivatva" (the state of being Śiva).
Thus, these qualities and attributes, being well-ascertained, should indeed be meditated upon by one who sings at the time of offering to the Supreme Lord,
or constantly while performing recitation (*japa*), together with the meanings of the case-endings, prefixes, particles, and verbal roots; thereafter,
in a very short time, purification and growth occur.
"And those [means] are to be personally experienced.
(GkT 1.6ab) Ritual procedure (*vidhi*) is the activity of the practitioner for the sake of the goal (*dharma*). (GkT 1.6ab) It is of two kinds: primary and secondary. (GkT 1.6ab)

In this context, that rule which is the cause of dharma (*dharma-hetu*) without any mediation is the primary one, and it will be called "conduct" (*caryā*). However, that which assists conduct is secondary, such as bathing and so forth. Among these, bathing (*snāna*) is for the purpose of removing the perception of unfitness caused by eating the leftovers of others and so forth, and for the purpose of manifesting one's spiritual marks (*liṅga*); whereas *upasparśana* (sipping water) is for the purpose of removing impurity.

Both of these [acts] must be performed with ashes alone, having contemplated the defects of saṃsāra by reflecting upon the command of the Lord, and having carefully considered the relative weight of the consequences. Even the wearing of the remains of offerings (nirmālya) supports one’s conduct by way of manifesting the Liṅga and increasing devotion. Having reflected on this, and having taken up the supreme, unattached remains of the Cause, the self-restrained person should [worship] the Cause.

Having prostrated, one should then request permission. Then, having meditated upon the Blessed One with a gracious countenance as he bestows his own remains (nirmālya) for the purpose of purification, and perceiving them as "Great Grace" (mahāprasāda), one should wear them on the head with devotion alone.
Likewise, even residing in a sacred precinct (āyatana) is a support for spiritual practice (caryā).
And so it has been said:
"For this is the supreme field of Dharma, the sanctuary of Śiva on earth;
it is the soil for the seed of ritual, and what is sown therein yields great fruit."
"A hundred cubits or more from the *liṅga* on all sides is the sacred field (*śivakṣetra*) of Śiva;
for living beings who die there, it is the cause of attaining union (*sāyujya*) with Śiva.
[GkT 1.6ab:72] "Whether in a village or elsewhere... and so forth. [GkT 1.6ab:73]
Prāṇāyāma is for the purpose of purifying the impurities that have not been washed away by the ritual sipping of water (*upasparśana*).
Prāṇāyāma is the restraint of the movement of the air within the body.

Having performed that sipping and having bowed down to the causes, the Tīrthakaras, and the teachers, one should face either the east or the north, assuming the lotus posture (*padmaka*), the cross-legged posture (*svastika*), or others.
Having assumed any posture at ease and having made it firm and elevated, one should gradually perform the exhalations (*recaka*) and so forth with an internally restrained mind.
Even when there is no turbidity [of the mind], one should practice constantly for the sake of attaining extreme purity of the mind and for the sake of cultivation.
For it has been said:
"One should burn away defects by means of breath-controls (prāṇāyāma), and sins by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā);
one should withdraw the sense-objects by means of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna). (GkT 1.6ab)
For the Brahmin who is disciplined in *prāṇāyāma* and whose self is restrained,
all defects perish and he becomes established in *sattva*.
He who might drink a drop of water from the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass month after month—

A full hundred years [of other practices] is equal to a single breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). Because one whose self is purified by breath-control perceives that Supreme Reality, there is a sacred tradition (*śruti*) stating: "There is nothing whatsoever superior to breath-control."
* For the purpose of exhausting the impurities that have not yet been exhausted, recitation (*japa*) should be performed.

* In either the third or the fourth *brahman*, one should repeatedly direct the mind—which has been restrained with effort—by means of the awareness of the complete syllables or the awareness of their meaning.
And thus, another penance (*prāyaścitta*) should not be performed because it would be outside the scope of the Sūtra.
Now, one might object: "The teaching of the three [vows] was indeed intended for the removal of defilement; but what penance is there for other transgressions?

It should not be said that "transgression is impossible for a vigilant ascetic because he is always self-restrained," for if that were so, it would follow that even the teaching of the three [vows] would never be undertaken, since [transgression] would be identical to the case of transgressions arising from desire and the like.
Furthermore, because of the power of demerit (*adharma*), even for a wise person, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is possible;
and it has been said: "Even while being conscious, one is carried away," and so forth.
And because violence is necessarily inevitable;
for it has been said:
"Whatever creatures a practitioner kills unknowingly by day and by night..."

Having bathed for the sake of their purification, one should perform six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) daily; this is the meaning. Here, some maintain that in all cases of transgression, only the triad [of breath-restraints] should be performed.

We, however, see that the triad must be performed solely for the purpose of removing defilement (*kaluṣa*). Since it is heard in the commentary (*bhāṣya*) that it is exactly so, it is not for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*); and because the purification of the unseen is uncertain, there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of never ceasing the triad. Therefore, once defilement has been removed, it is for the purpose of exhausting the demerit (*adharma*) produced by transgressions, just as previously accumulated demerit is exhausted.
Furthermore, one must indeed practice the observances (*vidhyācaraṇa*).
To this effect, the Sūtra says: "In that case, one should perform further austerity.
Manu also said:
Whatever sin people commit through speech, mind, or body,
those whose wealth is austerity quickly dispel it all by means of austerity alone—
even those who have committed great crimes (mahāpātakin) and others who have performed forbidden acts.
"By well-performed austerity alone, they are liberated from that sin.
Likewise, the illustrious author of the Bhāṣya has also stated an indicative proof:
"The noble ones drive away evil through austerities; by the application of meditation, they exhaust their merit."

Those stainless ones who know reality, being purified, go to liberation because of the absence of both [merit and demerit]. Nor is this a rule that meditation results only in the exhaustion of merit; rather, it also results in the exhaustion of demerit. For another explanatory statement has been made on that very point.
"Through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), one burns away the basis for all meritorious and non-meritorious actions;
when the fruits of merit and demerit have been burnt, no owner of them remains. Thus [it is said].

If it is argued that, in that case, the performance of the prescribed rule is useless, we say no; for the scripture states, "having gone into the presence of Rudra by means of this rule," and one who lacks the performance of the rule possesses no capacity for the practice of yoga.
Likewise, it is stated elsewhere:
"Dharma should be practiced with effort, especially by a yogin."
"Those who know Yoga understand that there is no Yoga apart from Dharma.

Therefore, having made the mind serene through ritual ablutions and other such means, one must— with absolute and constant application— perform the practice of the prescribed Yoga alone for the sake of exhausting all unrighteousness (adharma), and not some other form of expiation.

Likewise, when the ten restraints (*yama*), such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the rest, assist in spiritual practice (*caryā*), they are included within the category of injunctions (*vidhi*); however, when they assist in the performance of yoga (*yogakriyā*), they are included within yoga itself. In this regard, non-violence is the non-production of suffering in others through speech, body, or mind; celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is the restraint of the senses; truthfulness (*satya*) is the prohibition of speaking words that are not limbs of the means for achieving Dharma; non-conversation (*asaṃvyavahāra*) is the prohibition of social interaction with those belonging to the various castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramin*) who are not engaged in matters conducive to Dharma; [and so forth]. From the limb of the means for achieving Dharma...

Non-stealing (*asteya*) is the non-acceptance of what is extra according to the law, and by unjust means, even that which is a means for accomplishing *dharma*. Non-anger (*akrodha*) is the state of having an unclouded mind even when harmed by others. Service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) is behaving toward the teacher with a beneficial intent through speech, body, and mind. Purity (*śauca*) is the purification of the body and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). [Finally,] it is the consumption of food acquired solely through one’s own lawful occupation, in a manner that does not conflict with the performance of the application of *vidhi*.
Lightness of food:
some say that a sage should take eight morsels, but that is not accepted because it would result in a contradiction with the practice of the prescribed rules (*vidhi-yoga*).
Others hold that one should fill three parts of the stomach with solid food, side dishes, and water, and leave the fourth part for the movement of air.
This is indeed accepted because there is no contradiction.
And in this context, the statement describing the fivefold mendicancy, beginning with "he should practice the honey-gathering [mendicancy]," is to be explained without contradiction.
Vigilance (*apramāda*) consists in constant exertion in the performance of the yoga of the prescribed rules.
And this Yama is the primary [authority] in this regard.
Thus it has been said:
"Listen to the true nature of the dharma of the ascetic (yati), together with its virtues and defects."
"From heedfulness comes supreme accomplishment; from heedlessness, hell is certain.
Thus, even the wearing [of the marks] is indeed a prescription for virtue, because it assists the conduct by way of generating knowledge.
Yoga is the connection of the person (*puruṣa*) with the Lord (*īśvara*) by means of the mind (*citta*).

It is of two kinds: characterized by action (*kriyā-lakṣaṇa*) and characterized by the cessation of action (*kriyoparama-lakṣaṇa*). Among these, that characterized by action consists of recitation (*japa*), restraint (*yantraṇa*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and remembrance (*smaraṇa*).
We shall explain this.
Although characterized by the cessation of activity, it is also denoted by terms such as "transcendence" (*atigati*) and so forth.
The "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) consists in the designation of these [categories] as superior to the categories mentioned in other treatises.

For instance, in another treatise, the "end of suffering" (*duḥkhānta*) is defined as the mere cessation of suffering; here, however, it is the attainment of supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvaryaprāpti*).
Likewise, elsewhere an effect (*kārya*) is something that comes into being after not having existed; here, however, the "flock" (*paśu*) and so forth are eternal.
Similarly, elsewhere the cause is something dependent, such as *pradhāna* and the like; here, however, the Lord (*bhagavān*) alone is independent.
* Likewise, elsewhere yoga has liberation (*kaivalya*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) as its fruit, but here it has the ultimate end of suffering (*paramaduḥkhānta*) as its fruit.
* Likewise, elsewhere the injunction (*vidhi*) leads to rebirth with heaven and so forth as its fruit, but here it does not lead to rebirth, having proximity to Rudra and so forth as its fruit.

* Regarding the "conclusion and withdrawal of categories" (*padārthānāṃ samāptisaṃhāra*), the word "therein" (*tatra*) refers to suffering, effects, causes, and injunctions; by the word "conclusion," their cessation is expressed.

"But [the conclusion] is for the sake of [indicating] the completion of the yoga by means of the word 'iti'. (GkT 1.6ab:128) "The statement of another property (*dharmāntara*) is the conclusion (*nigamana*), for the purpose of making those [properties] complete and exhaustive, and for the purpose of removing incidental doubts.
(GkT 1.6ab:129) "Others [say it is] for the purpose of demonstrating that [the conclusion] forms a single syntactical unit with the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). (GkT 1.6ab:130)

Thus, although injunction (*vidhi*) and application (*yoga*) are included within the [other] categories (*kārya*), they are mentioned separately due to their great importance; therefore, the compendia of the five alone have been stated, and so only five categories (*padārtha*) are spoken of.
Others, however, describe the divisions of the categories in another way.
*Tattva*, *guṇa*, and *bhāva*—these are the [categories].
Among them, that which is independent (*anāśrita*) is *tattva*.
And it is of twenty varieties.
The five [elements] beginning with earth, the thirteen organs, and the cause (the individual soul) constitute the animal.

Regarding the categories of reality, the qualities (guṇas) which depend on the states of being exist there within the elements such as earth according to their possibility; specifically, the five—form, taste, smell, touch, and sound—subsist [in them].
However, the principles of the sense organs are devoid of qualities.

In the bound souls (*paśu*), seven qualities (*guṇa*) exist, characterized by the nature of being a bound soul (*paśutva*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), consciousness (*citta*), knowledge (*vidyā*), effort (*prayatna*), and desire (*icchā*). (GkT 1.6ab) However, because pleasure and the other [qualities] are modifications of those [seven], they are included within them, just like the modifications of clay. (GkT 1.6ab) In the cause (*kāraṇa*), there are three qualities known as desire (*kāma*), seeking (*arthitva*), and ignorance (*vipratva*); these are indefinable in terms of being either different or non-different from the substrata (*dharmi*). (GkT 1.6ab)
The properties (*dharma*) of the qualities (*guṇa*) are called "entities" (*bhāva*).
And since the investigation of those [entities] has already been performed during the investigation of the pre-existent effect (*satkārya*), it is not done here.
Thus, the knowledge that ascertains the cause and so forth is the first attainment.
He states the second gain as "asceticism" (*tapas*).
That dharma produced by the rules for ash-baths and so forth is called asceticism.
Its arising is also determined from signs such as its preservation.

The practitioner, being carried away from the true path by the thief of unrighteousness (*adharmataskara*), is protected by Dharma, which stands in the place of a city guardian. (GkT 1.6ab:148) Movement (*gati*) is the transition from one state to another state. (GkT 1.6ab:149) Contentment (*prīti*) is satisfaction in the very performance of what has been prescribed. (GkT 1.6ab:150)

* Acquisition (*prāpti*) is the connection with gain. (GkT 1.6ab) The meaning is that its majesty, which is the power of *dharma*, is that by whose force the mind of one intent on the practice of the method cannot be disturbed even by the songs and instrumental music of Rambhā and others. (GkT 1.6ab) The terms "transcendence" (*atigati*), "union" (*sāyujya*), and "abiding" (*sthiti*) are synonyms for the state of culmination (*niṣṭhāyoga*). (GkT 1.6ab)

That in whose presence objects become perceptible to the practitioner through direct perception is illumination (*prakāśa*). It is twofold, distinguished as the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*).

Among these, that by which one correctly discerns the means for the practice of the method (*vidhi-yoga*), and perceives one's own mind when it is concentrated, has strayed, or is in the process of straying from the reality to be meditated upon—namely, Brahman—is the lower illumination.

But he who, at the time of establishing [the practice], perceives all principles (*tattva*) along with their qualities as infinite and discriminates between what is to be joined and what is not to be joined, is the Supreme (*para*). Just as for those possessing sense objects there is a flow of mental fluctuations toward desired objects, so too for one who does not desire [them], there is a flow of mental fluctuations toward Rudra; that very state, having reached its ultimate excellence, is "permanence in the divine" (*devanityatva*). All this has been stated by way of making known the nature of Dharma.
He states the third gain:
"Now, permanence.

The word "now" (*atha*) indicates immediate succession; immediately after austerity, that which is permanence—characterized by the cultivation of the state of being [the deity] within the god—is called the third gain.
But the meaning is not "perpetual conjunction.
Here, "permanence" (*nityatva*) is intended in the sense of an uninterrupted flow, just as one says, "the Ganges has a perpetual flow.
He states the fourth attainment as "stability" (*sthiti*).
When the mind has severed the web of causes of the defects and the cessation of what is called its root occurs, its abiding in Rudra—its absolute immobility—is termed "stability" (sthiti).
Simultaneously with that, nine characteristics such as non-attachment arise for the yogin.
Among these, non-attachment is the absolute turning away from attachment, which is being observed.
Yogitva is the state of the true nature of consciousness (cittattva) abiding solely within the principle of Rudra (*kevalarudratattva*).
Nityātmatva is the state of the mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*) being in accordance [with that reality].
Ajatva is the state of consciousness being non-manifesting (*aprādurbhāvin*).
Supreme equanimity is loving-kindness (*maitratva*).
Freedom from the body and so forth is oneness (*ekatva*).

He states the fifth impurity as "the state of being a bound soul" (*paśutva*). (GkT 1.8:25) The state of being a bound soul is a quality of the person (*puruṣaguṇa*) distinct from merit and demerit, which is to be inferred from its resistance [to liberation]. (GkT 1.8:26) And that [state], though endowed with fourteen characteristics, constitutes impurity (*malatva*). (GkT 1.8:27)
And those characteristics, beginning with non-omniscience and ending with non-liberation, have been explained precisely as the opposites of omniscience and the rest.
Thinking that such a state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*) is the primordial cause of saṃsāra and constitutes its primary substance, he calls it the "root.
For even in the case of those who have attained isolation (*kaivalya*), although other impurities are absent, they would fall back into saṃsāra solely because of this state of being a bound soul.
"Five" is for the purpose of concluding [the enumeration] by excluding both deficiency and excess.
"These" is for the purpose of restriction.
The meaning is that these alone are the impurities consisting of the bondage of saṃsāra, and not the relationship between the enjoyer and the enjoyed and so forth as stated in other scriptures.
Where, then, are such impurities (mala) well-known? To this he says:
"In the Tantra. This means that in the scripture known as the Tantra—which was directly composed by Maheśvara, beginning with the word *atha* and ending with *śiva*—these [impurities] are expounded.

Anticipating the objection that since even virtue (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and so forth are abandoned, they too would incur the status of being impurities just like unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the like, he says: "By virtue of being within the scope of what is to be abandoned (*heyādhikārataḥ*)."
Those things which, like mud and so forth, are considered causes of suffering such that the practitioner is authorized to exert effort for their elimination—

these alone are impurities (*mala*), and not those which, like flowers and so forth, perish even against one's will. Therefore, because they fall within the domain of what is to be abandoned (*heya*), ignorance (*ajñāna*) and the rest are indeed the impurities.
Alternatively, there is the reading *heyādhikārikāḥ*; in that case as well, this is the meaning:

those who possess (*adhikāra*) the fitness (*yogyatā*) for abandonment—that is, for being eliminated (*kṣapaṇīya*) by way of being objects to be abandoned (*heyatvena*)—are "those whose office is abandonment" (*heyādhikāriṇaḥ*), and these very ones are *heyādhikārikāḥ*.
The suffix *-ka* is used here in its own sense (to form an adjective from the preceding noun).

Alternatively, by adding the suffix *ikaṅ* to the word *adhikāra*, a *karmadhāraya* compound is formed with the word *heya*. Thus, the meaning is that here only those impurities (*mala*) which pertain to the category of the "reprehensible" (*heyādhikārika*) are intended.
Therefore, even qualities such as merit (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and dispassion (*vairāgya*) are not considered impurities.
All of this has been explained by me in brief, like the ocean.
Through the grace of the teachers, one attains the knowledge characterized by the fivefold purpose. (1.8.43) What is the use of knowing many scriptures that obstruct one's own practice?
Having known this alone as supreme, one should become devoted to the practice of yoga. (1.8.44)

But this knowledge should be given to one who, upon hearing this, considers himself to have accomplished his purpose; it should not be given to anyone else by one desiring success. However, if someone should give it to those devoid of moral discipline for any reason whatsoever, [he incurs great fault].
He would go to a lower state along with his disciples due to the betrayal of secrets. Homage to that true Guru, who has reached the end of all sciences,
by whom the ocean of the five-fold meaning was revealed through these eight excellent verses.
